title: NHL Overtime and Shootout Rules for Bettors in Canada
excerpt: Understand how NHL overtime and shootouts affect moneyline, puck line, totals and props so Canadian bettors avoid settlement surprises this season.
author: Lisa Davids
bodyHtml:
Few things frustrate hockey bettors more than a wager that looks like a winner until the final horn, then settles differently than expected because of overtime or a shootout. Understanding NHL overtime and shootout rules for betting in Canada is one of the cheapest edges available, because it costs nothing and prevents avoidable mistakes. This guide explains how regular-season and playoff extra time work, how the main markets treat it, and what to check before you place a bet.

How NHL Extra Time Works

In the regular season, a game that is tied after three periods goes to a short overtime period played with fewer skaters per side. If nobody scores, the game moves to a shootout, and one team is awarded the win. The shootout means regular-season games cannot end in a tie. Playoff hockey is different: teams play full sudden-death overtime periods until someone scores, with no shootout at all.

That difference matters for betting because a regular-season game can be decided by a skills contest, which has little to do with how the teams played for sixty minutes. A market that includes the shootout can therefore be settled by something that was not part of the main game.

Moneyline: Usually Includes Everything

The standard NHL moneyline normally settles on the final result, including overtime and the shootout. If you back a team at the moneyline and they win in a shootout, your bet is a winner. That is why a moneyline can sometimes look shorter than you expect: the price reflects the possibility of winning after regulation.

Some sportsbooks also offer a three-way or regulation-time moneyline, where you bet on home, away or a tie after sixty minutes. In that market, a game that goes to overtime settles as a draw, regardless of who wins later. These prices can look attractive for the underdog or the draw option, but you are betting on a different event. Always read the market name carefully.

Puck Line and Totals

The puck line is hockey's version of a point spread, typically set at 1.5 goals. Overtime and shootout results usually count, but a shootout win is recorded as a one-goal margin, which has a big effect on puck line outcomes. A team that wins by a single goal in a shootout generally cannot cover a -1.5 puck line, while an underdog at +1.5 covers in that same scenario. For more detail, our guide to puck line betting in Canada breaks down how those bets behave.

Totals bets usually include overtime goals but treat the shootout differently. In most cases, shootout goals do not count toward the total. If a game is tied 3-3 and the game-winning shootout goal is awarded as the 4-3 final, the sportsbook generally settles totals on the 3-3 score. Rules vary, so verify them before wagering.

Why the Details Change the Value

Because overtime and shootouts can swing results, a bettor who understands the settlement rules can sometimes spot a mispriced line. For example, teams that frequently play tight, low-scoring games may see more extra-time contests. That can matter when you decide between the moneyline and the regulation market, or between backing a favourite on the puck line versus the straight win.

Period and Prop Markets

Period betting normally settles on the specific period only. Overtime is not part of the third period, so a first-period or third-period total will not count extra-time goals. Player props can be trickier. Goals, assists and shots on goal usually count overtime activity but not shootout attempts, though sportsbooks do not all follow the same convention. Check the rules of the specific prop and look for wording about overtime and shootouts.

  • Moneyline: typically includes overtime and the shootout.
  • Regulation-time (three-way): a tie after sixty minutes settles as a draw.
  • Puck line: includes extra time, with the shootout winner recorded as one goal ahead.
  • Totals: usually include overtime goals but not shootout goals.
  • Period bets: settle on that period alone.
  • Player props: check whether overtime counts and whether shootout attempts are excluded.

Live Betting in Overtime

In-play markets add another layer. During regulation, a tie score can lead to a rapidly changing moneyline, and in overtime the short period and reduced skater numbers produce volatile pricing. Some books suspend markets frequently in overtime or limit the available bet types. If you enjoy live wagering, be prepared for narrower options and quicker line movement, and avoid chasing a loss with a rushed overtime bet.

Playoff Overtime Is a Different Game

Once the playoffs begin, full-length overtime periods replace the shootout. A game can go very long, which affects totals, props and live markets. Totals bettors should recognise that longer games increase the chance of the over cashing, while fatigue and reduced scoring chances can change how late-game periods play out. Because playoff overtime continues until a goal, a moneyline bet is decided by actual hockey rather than a skills contest.

Where to Read the Rules

Every sportsbook publishes house rules, typically linked in the footer or the help section. Search for the hockey section and note how it treats overtime, shootouts, postponed games and player props. Compare wording between operators using our Canadian sportsbook listings, and if you play in Ontario, our Ontario betting guide explains how the regulated market handles standards and complaints. For Alberta bettors, the Alberta page covers the local picture.

Practical Habits for Hockey Bettors

Read the market title before confirming a slip, especially when a three-way or regulation market sits next to the standard moneyline. Screenshot your bet slip so you have a record of what you selected. Keep totals and puck line bets in mind when tracking results, because a shootout can turn a seemingly comfortable ticket into a loser. Finally, set a staking plan before the season begins and stick to it. Hockey's variance is high even for informed bettors, and knowing the rules improves your decisions but does not guarantee profit.

Key Takeaways

NHL overtime and shootout rules shape how nearly every hockey market is settled. The moneyline usually counts everything, regulation markets treat extra time as a tie, the puck line records a shootout win as a single goal, and totals often ignore shootout goals. Spend two minutes reading the rules before you bet, compare how different books phrase them, and treat the details as part of your edge rather than small print to be skipped.
